subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If n is a positive integer, show that (1 + cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ + (1 + cos θ − i sin θ)ⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ cosⁿ(θ/2) cos(nθ/2).

mark_split.label: Half-angle form of 1 + cos θ + i sin θ
Raise to n by De Moivre's theorem

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how the half-angle identities rewrite 1 + cos θ + i sin θ, what De Moivre's theorem does to it, and how the two powers combine.
insider_note: Two of the seven marks are for the half-angle rewrite alone. Students who jump straight to De Moivre without taking 2cos(θ/2) outside lose them and get the wrong power.

steps.label: Half-angle form of 1 + cos θ + i sin θ
steps.margin_note: First and second marks. 1 + cos θ = 2cos²(θ/2) and sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2), so 2cos(θ/2) comes out as a common factor and leaves cos(θ/2) + i sin(θ/2). Here r is the expression 2cos(θ/2), not a number from a square root.

recall.must_convey: That 1 + cos θ + i sin θ is rewritten with half angles as 2cos(θ/2) times (cos(θ/2) + i sin(θ/2)).
accept: use one plus cos theta equals two cos squared theta by two and sin theta equals two sin theta by two cos theta by two
take out two cos theta by two so the bracket is cos theta by two plus i sin theta by two
write it in half angles as two cos theta by two times cis theta by two
half angle formulas use chesi two cos theta by two bayataki teeyali
the modulus is two cos theta by two and the amplitude is theta by two

steps.why: The number is not in cos + i sin form as given. The half-angle identities turn 1 + cos θ into 2cos²(θ/2) and sin θ into 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2), and the common factor 2cos(θ/2) is exactly the r that De Moivre's theorem needs outside the bracket.
common_mistakes: Using 1 + cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), the wrong half-angle identity.
Taking out cos(θ/2) but forgetting the 2, which loses the 2ⁿ later.
Trying to find r as √(...) numerically; here r is the expression 2cos(θ/2).

steps.label: Raise to n by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. Raising to n gives 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) outside and cos(nθ/2) + i sin(nθ/2) inside. The n on cos(θ/2) sits outside the bracket and the n on the angle sits inside; they are two separate places.

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem is applied: raising the mod-amp form to the power n multiplies the angle by n and gives 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) (cos(nθ/2) + i sin(nθ/2)), called equation (1).
accept: apply De Moivre's theorem so the angle is multiplied by n and we get 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) (cos(nθ/2) + i sin(nθ/2))
raise the mod amp form to the power and multiply the angle by n by De Moivre
by De Moivre cos theta plus i sin theta to the power gives cos n theta plus i sin n theta
De Moivre theorem apply chesi angle ni n tho multiply cheyyali
the power goes onto the angle by De Moivre's theorem, that is equation one

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem says (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n: the power moves onto the angle. The real factor r is raised separately, as an ordinary real number.
common_mistakes: Raising the bracket by De Moivre but forgetting to raise 2cos(θ/2) to n as well.
Writing cos(nθ/2) as cosⁿ(θ/2) inside the bracket; the power on cos(θ/2) is outside, the n on the angle is inside.
Writing (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cosⁿ θ + i sinⁿ θ, which is false.

steps.label: The conjugate power
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. The second bracket is the conjugate of the first, so it carries the same 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) with the sine sign reversed. Label it (2); nothing is recomputed.

recall.must_convey: That the conjugate number is treated in the same way and gives 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) (cos(nθ/2) − i sin(nθ/2)), called equation (2), with the sign of the sine term changed.
accept: similarly the conjugate gives the same thing with minus i sin, that is equation two
do the same for the conjugate and only the sign of the sine changes
the second bracket is the conjugate so its power is 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) (cos(nθ/2) − i sin(nθ/2))
conjugate ki same step, sin term sign matrame minus avuthundi
equation two is the conjugate with cos minus i sin

steps.why: The second number is the conjugate of the first, so it has the same r and the angle −θ. Nothing new has to be computed; only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Recomputing r and θ from scratch and losing time.
Writing equation (2) without the minus sign, so nothing cancels in the next step.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Adding (1) and (2) cancels the i sin terms and doubles the cosine: 2ⁿ cosⁿ(θ/2) · 2 cos(nθ/2). Combine 2ⁿ · 2 into 2ⁿ⁺¹.
lines: (1 + cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ + (1 + cos θ − i sin θ)ⁿ

recall.must_convey: That equations (1) and (2) are added, the i sin terms cancel, and the result is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cosⁿ(θ/2) cos(nθ/2).
accept: add one and two, the i sin terms cancel and we get 2ⁿ⁺¹ cosⁿ(θ/2) cos(nθ/2)
adding the two equations the sine parts cancel leaving two times the cosine
one plus two gives two cos and the final answer is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cosⁿ(θ/2) cos(nθ/2)
rendu equations add cheste sin terms cancel ayyi 2ⁿ⁺¹ cosⁿ(θ/2) cos(nθ/2) vasthundi
the imaginary parts cancel on adding and the answer is two to the n plus one times cos

steps.why: The two numbers are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part. Adding removes the i sin terms and leaves exactly the cosine the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Subtracting instead of adding, which leaves 2i sin instead of 2 cos.
Leaving the answer as 2ⁿ · 2 cos instead of combining into one power of 2.
Dropping the factor that comes from r, which is the whole reason the answer has a power of 2.
